title: What happens to the HCF when both numbers are doubled?
description: The highest common factor of two hundred seventy and fifty is found from their primes, and then the same is done for the doubled numbers, five hundred forty and one hundred. The extra two in both numbers lands in the shared part, so the highest common factor doubles. Keeko doubts this and thinks it stays ten.
teaching_notes: One idea: doubling both numbers gives each one an extra two, and that two is shared, so the highest common factor doubles. Watch for students who think the highest common factor stays the same because both numbers changed in the same way.

source: Find the HCF of 270 and 50, and then of the doubled numbers 540 and 100. What do you see?
video_script.why: The child can find a highest common factor from the primes and now sees how it changes when both numbers are doubled.
video_script.substitution: Doubling a number adds one extra two to its primes, and an extra two in both numbers is shared, so it joins the highest common factor.
video_script.anchor: The pairs 270 and 50, and 540 and 100, written one under the other with the prime products beside them.
video_script.wrong_answer: the highest common factor stays ten
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks both numbers are doubled in the same way, so the highest common factor stays ten, but each number gains an extra two and that two is shared, which makes the highest common factor twenty.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor doubles from ten to twenty

final_answer.value: The HCF of 270 and 50 is 10 and of 540 and 100 is 20; it doubles
final_answer.spoken: ten for the first pair and twenty for the doubled pair

never_show: 10 as the HCF of 540 and 100, marked right
maths_rules: each number gained one extra 2, and that 2 is shared, so the HCF doubled from 10 to 20
slip: both numbers are doubled so the HCF stays 10; but 10 does not hold the extra 2 that both numbers now have
video_script.design: One idea: doubling both numbers adds a shared two, so the highest common factor doubles. The two pairs stay on the board from step one to the answer.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Doubling a number means multiplying it by two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six is two times three, and its double is twelve, which is two times two times three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Doubling adds one extra two to the primes.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, write each number as a product of primes. Two hundred seventy has one two, three threes and one five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Fifty has one two and two fives.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>They share one two and one five, which multiply to ten.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, do the same for the doubled numbers. Five hundred forty has two twos, three threes and one five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred has two twos and two fives.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>They share two twos and one five.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, compare the two pairs. Each number gained one extra two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That extra two is in both numbers, so it joins the shared part.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks both numbers are doubled, so the highest common factor stays ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But doubling puts an extra two in each number, and ten has no room for it.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The extra two is shared, so the highest common factor grows. The answer stays twenty.
